primary_claim: Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP) — appending synthetic, constitution-grounded, first-person moral reflections to 10% of pretraining documents from the start of pretraining ('Token Zero') — produces a 1.7B-parameter model with 1.7% mean attack success rate across five adversarial jailbreak benchmarks, a 63% reduction versus a data-matched unfiltered baseline, and shows 'persona binding': the post-trained model still cites a value-constitution article held out entirely from post-training data (citation rates 4-41%, vs. 0% for the baseline), though this binding is brittle and disappears when post-training uses a different assistant/chat template than pretraining used.

effect.metric: mean/max attack success rate (ASR) across JailbreakBench, AdvBench, PAP, DANs, PEZ; held-out charter article citation rate
effect.value: SPP (Token Zero): 1.7% mean ASR, a 63% reduction vs. unfiltered Baseline; template-matched mixSFT: 62% reduction; template-mismatched mixSFT: SPP provides no benefit (ASR +8% vs baseline); persona binding: held-out article citation 4-41% for SPP vs 0% for Baseline; toxic-filtering-only baselines were same or slightly less safe than unfiltered baseline

depends_on: Persona Selection Model (Marks et al. 2026, alignment.anthropic.com/2026/psm)
JailbreakBench, AdvBench, PAP, DANs, PEZ benchmarks
Aydin et al. 2026 Model Raising framework
contradicts_or_qualifies: subtractive pretraining-safety approaches (data filtering, e.g. Deep Ignorance, SafeLM-style rewriting) which the authors find do not improve and can slightly reduce safety compared to unfiltered baselines

the implicit assumption in prior work (e.g. Model Spec Midtraining) that concentrating alignment interventions into a midtraining cooldown stage is sufficient — the paper finds integrating reflections from Token Zero outperforms a token-matched midtraining-only variant
stated_future_work: evaluate robustness to benign fine-tuning attacks and continued fine-tuning more broadly
scale runs to 3B parameters and 500B tokens, and implement SPP at production scale with the Apertus model team
test whether persona binding survives adversarial fine-tuning or merely raises the cost of undoing alignment
investigate what determines binding success/failure and whether bridging reflection/post-training distributions (e.g. combining with Model Spec Midtraining) reduces brittleness
study how post-SFT reinforcement learning affects persona binding
mechanistically analyze SPP's effect in activation space using interpretability tools
determine optimal reflection density and whether reflections on benign content are necessary
add missing baselines: reflections-as-summaries control, SafeLM-style rephrasing, explicit refusal demonstrations in reflections
limitations_stated: preliminary results at 1.7B parameters and 100B tokens, well below the frontier; capability-hit assessment is hard to make definitively at this scale
have not yet evaluated robustness to benign fine-tuning attacks or continued fine-tuning, the most obvious stress test for a pretraining-time alignment method
persona binding is brittle: strength depends heavily on distributional match (same assistant token/template) between pretraining and post-training; a template mismatch eliminates the benefit entirely

SPP-trained models were the most susceptible to abliteration (projecting out the refusal direction), suggesting SPP concentrates safety into an easily-found-and-removed linear direction — a real attack surface under white-box access
the Persona Selection Model theoretical framing may degrade as a description of longer post-training phases, per its own authors
no established science yet on how to make persona binding succeed reliably or predict when it will
quote: Injecting reflections from the start of pretraining (Token Zero) yields 1.7% mean ASR, a 63% reduction over the Baseline... SPP (Token Zero, dark red) still cites the held-out article at rates between 4% and 41%, despite never encountering it during post-training.
